Meta.siteTitle: Whygrid - poker tournament reviews with an AI coach
Meta.siteDescription: A Socratic AI coach for tournament poker. The parser crunches your hands exactly, and the coach leads with questions - until you see for yourself where you're losing chips. Your first tournament review is free.
Meta.pricingDescription: Your first tournament review in Whygrid is free. After that, a subscription with a review-dialogue of your own hands: the coach leads with questions, the parser does the numbers. No hidden charges.
Meta.howToExportDescription: Step by step: how to turn on hand-history saving and find the files in GGPoker, PokerStars, Winamax, 888poker, ACR / PokerKing, Red Star Poker (iPoker) and BetOnline (Chico), so you can upload a tournament to Whygrid for review.

HowToExport.title: How to export your hands
HowToExport.intro: A review is built from the hand-history files from your poker client. It's nearly the same everywhere: you turn on history saving in the settings once, find the folder with the files, and upload them to us. The room is detected automatically, opponents' nicknames are anonymized, and the first review is free. You can upload several files at once. Pick your room:

Landing.heroTitle: Stop losing money on the same mistakes
Landing.heroSubtitle: The same leaks show up tournament after tournament and cost you real money. Whygrid finds them in your own hands and guides you with questions until you see where you spilled chips yourself - instead of memorizing someone else's advice.
Landing.freeFirstNote: No card required - your first tournament is reviewed free
Landing.alternativesSubtitle: Poker mistakes get fixed by review. The only question is which kind.
Landing.altConsultationDescription: About $50 for a single review. Almost no one reviews micro stakes systematically.
Landing.altSelfDescription: You might misread a spot, never find the answer, or mistake someone else's leak for a rule - cementing the mistake instead of fixing it.
Landing.altWhygridDescription: Your own hands. The parser does the math exactly, and the coach leads with questions - until you see where you spilled chips yourself.
Landing.benefitNumbersDescription: VPIP, chip losses, position - computed by a deterministic parser. The numbers are always right; the AI never makes them up.
Landing.benefitMethodTitle: A question, not a ready answer
Landing.benefitMethodDescription: You're led to the solution with Socratic questions - you see the mistake and remember it yourself, instead of cramming someone else's tip.
Landing.benefitGameDescription: Not abstract textbook spots, but the exact hands you played yourself.
Landing.step1Description: Sign up and drop in a tournament hand-history file from any major poker room - the first one is reviewed free. The parser walks through every hand.
Landing.step2Description: On a couple of the most debatable hands, the coach asks why you played it that way - before giving any verdict.
Landing.step3Description: Compare your answer with the review - and see for yourself where your logic didn't match what happened at the table.
Landing.objectionExpensiveAnswer: Cheaper than a single coaching session. One pot you don't spill over the long run pays for a month of the subscription.
Landing.objectionDoubtAnswer: Don't take our word for it. Upload a tournament - the first review is free, and judge by your own hands.
Landing.objectionSelfAnswer: You know the theory. The question is whether you see your recurring leaks across dozens of tournaments - that's exactly what the review shows.
Landing.finalSubtitle: The first tournament is reviewed free. Upload your hand-history file - and see for yourself where you spill chips while the coach leads you with questions.
Landing.previewSituationLine1End: on the button. You 3-bet, the BB calls.
Landing.previewSituationLine2End: . Your opponent bets the whole pot. You call.
Landing.previewCoachQuestion: What did you pay for on the river? Which of your opponent's hands do you beat here?

networkLabels.ipoker: iPoker network - also Betfair, Betsson and others

notes.ggpoker: GGPoker has no "download everything at once" button. If you played different formats (tournaments, Spin & Gold), go through each section on the left separately.
notes.pokerstars: Want to see the hand right at the table - enable "Instant Hand History" in the table menu ("Table"). The history language doesn't matter, we read any.
notes.winamax: Windows hides the AppData folder - in Explorer turn on "Show hidden items" (the "View" tab), otherwise you won't find it. Winamax won't let you change the history folder - take the files from this one.
notes.ipoker: The client must be in English - otherwise the history might not save correctly. Windows hides the AppData folder - turn on showing hidden items.
notes.chico: If some file isn't recognized - let us know and we'll fix it.

pokerstars: The path is shown in "Where To Save" in the same settings
chico: the folder you set in the history settings

ggpoker: Open the GGPoker client and sign in.
At the top of the window find the history icon (a list/clock symbol) and click it - a panel of recent events opens.
At the bottom of that panel click "PokerCraft…" - it's the analytics built into the client.
In the PokerCraft window pick "Tournament" in the left menu - the list of tournaments you played appears.
At the top, in the "Date" filter, set a period (e.g. "Last 7 days") and click the red "SHOW" button.
To the left of a tournament tick the checkbox (the checkbox at the column header selects all of them at once).
Click the RED "Setup - game histories" button. The green "Game results" next to it is only the summary, not the hands - it won't work.
A file downloads. If it's an archive (.zip) - unpack it, the .txt files are inside. Upload those to us.
pokerstars: Open the PokerStars client and sign in.
On the left pick "Playing History" → "Hand History".
Tick "Save My Hand History" - without it the files aren't written.
Right there, the "Where To Save" field shows the folder with the files. Note it down (or click "Change Folder" and pick a convenient one).
Open that folder on your computer and grab the tournament .txt files you need.
winamax: Open the Winamax client and sign in.
Open "User Settings" - usually a gear icon or a menu item with your nickname.
Go to the "Game settings" tab → "Hand History".
Open the profile folder (path below) and grab the .txt files.
888poker: Open the 888poker client (lobby) and sign in.
Tick "Keep my hand history in" - save the hand history.
The folder is shown next to it (to change it - the "Change Folder" button). Note the path.
Open that folder and grab the tournament .txt files.
acr: Open the client (Americas Cardroom or PokerKing) and sign in.
Click the settings gear in the top-right corner → "Hand Histories" in the left menu. Another way: "Game Info" at the top → "View Hand History" → the "Options" button at the bottom.
Look at the "Destination folder" field - that's the folder with the files.
Open that folder and grab the .txt files.
ipoker: Open the Red Star Poker client (or another iPoker room) and sign in.
In the lobby open "My Account" → "Settings" → the "General" section.
Open the folder with the files (path below; the client name in the path is your room).
Grab the hand-history files - they're .xml or .txt.
chico: Open the BetOnline client (or TigerGaming / SportsBetting) and sign in.
In the lobby, bottom left, open "Settings" → "More options".
In the "History" section enable "Save Hand History" and set the folder to save the hands to.
Play - the .txt files land in that folder. Open it and grab the ones you need.

Glossary.helpLabel: What the metrics and abbreviations mean
Glossary.title: What the abbreviations mean
Glossary.srDescription: Explanation of metrics and poker abbreviations
Glossary.vpipDesc: How often you voluntarily enter the pot preflop - by calling or raising (blinds don't count). A rough measure of how loose you play: high means many hands, low means tight.
Glossary.pfrDesc: How often you enter the pot by raising preflop. The gap between VPIP and PFR shows how much you just call instead of applying pressure with a raise.
Glossary.rfiDesc: Opening with a raise when no one has entered the pot before you. The "opener" is exactly this RFI. Each position has its own normal opening range.
Glossary.sprDesc: The ratio of the effective stack to the pot on the flop. A small SPR means the pot is already big relative to stacks, so it's easier to commit; a big one leaves room to maneuver.
Glossary.bbDesc: Stack and hand result are measured in big blinds: "15 BB" is clearer than "383,304 chips" because it doesn't depend on the blind level.
Glossary.afDesc: How many aggressive actions after the flop (bet, raise) you make per passive one (call). Higher means you play the hand more aggressively.
Glossary.potOddsDesc: How much you have to put in relative to what's already in the pot. You compare it with your chances to improve to decide whether the call is profitable.

ReferenceCharts.title: Charts
ReferenceCharts.intro: The reference ranges your coach judges your play against. This is the baseline; how you actually open is shown in "Your charts" on "My tournaments".
ReferenceCharts.openIntro: Which hands to open the pot with when everyone folds to you. Pick a position.
ReferenceCharts.sbNote: On the small blind this is the raising range. Weak hands aren't folded when it's folded to you - they limp, a separate legitimate line.
ReferenceCharts.legendAlways: Always open - the core of the range
ReferenceCharts.legendSometimes: Sometimes, depending on the spot (roughly half the time)
ReferenceCharts.legendBorder: Borderline: not a mistake, but not a recommendation - the coach won't flag these
ReferenceCharts.disclaimer: This is not GTO solver output - these are your coach's working ranges for micro-stakes tournaments. The core matches solver ranges; in early positions our ranges are softer than the solver's - the coach only punishes clearly loose opens, not borderline hands. Want to play tighter - stick to the solid lime zone.
ReferenceCharts.depthNote: Baseline for stacks of 20 big blinds and deeper: shorter stacks are push-fold territory. Deeper than 60 blinds the edges can widen slightly.
ReferenceCharts.pushIntro: Which hands to go all-in with first when everyone folds to you. Pick a stack and a position.
ReferenceCharts.pushLegendAlways: Push - the hand is in the all-in range
ReferenceCharts.pushDisclaimer: These ranges are taken from Nash push-fold charts and checked against public ones: this spot is solved math, there are no solver disagreements here. From 15 blinds push-fold no longer applies - that's regular opening territory (chart above). HJ plays the CO chart.
ReferenceCharts.bbIntro: How to respond from the BB to a single open of about 2.5 blinds. Pick the opener's position - the later it is, the wider the defense.
ReferenceCharts.bbLegendThreebetBluff: 3-bet bluff at a frequency - allowed, not required; the coach won't flag it
ReferenceCharts.bbLegendCallSometimes: Call sometimes, depending on the spot
ReferenceCharts.bbDisclaimer: An average of solver charts and a practical micro-stakes baseline: thin solver "junk" at the calling edges is trimmed - it doesn't make money against weak fields. The coach only flags 3-bets clearly wider than this boundary. Defense against a small-blind open is a different spot and isn't judged by this chart.
ReferenceCharts.vsOpenTitle: 3-betting vs an open (not from the BB)
ReferenceCharts.vsOpenIntro: Which hands to 3-bet a single open with when you're not in the big blind. Pick your position.
ReferenceCharts.vsOpenLegendOut: 3-bet not recommended: call or fold depending on the spot
ReferenceCharts.vsOpenDisclaimer: The most nuanced preflop spot, so the chart only judges the 3-bet: cold calling is deliberately not graded - it depends heavily on position, opponent and depth. The coach only flags 3-bets clearly wider than the boundary.
ReferenceCharts.isoIntro: Which hands to isolate a limper with. Pick your position.
ReferenceCharts.isoLegendOverlimp: Small pair: overlimp - isolating with it counts as a mistake
ReferenceCharts.isoDisclaimer: Isolation is almost the opening range, but slightly tighter: small pairs 22-66 are better off just limping along (set-mining cheaply), and the junky bottom folds. Against several limpers or with a big sizing isolate even tighter.

PlayerCharts.empty: Nothing to show yet - upload and review tournaments to build the picture of your game.
PlayerCharts.bbIntro: Against a single open: what you call with and what you 3-bet with, by the opener's position. Calls aren't judged - only 3-bets clearly wider than the norm light up in lime.
PlayerCharts.vsOpenTitle: How you play against an open
PlayerCharts.vsOpenIntro: You're not in the BB, facing a single open: cold calls and 3-bets by your position. Calls aren't judged - only 3-bets clearly wider than the norm light up in lime.
PlayerCharts.isoIntro: Raises over a limp by your position. Isolations clearly wider than the norm light up in lime.
PlayerCharts.pushIntro: All-in first into the pot with under 15 BB, by position and stack depth. Shoves wider than the norm light up in lime.
PlayerCharts.legendJudgedWide: {noun} wider than the norm - worth a look
PlayerCharts.legendJudgedThin: {noun} wider than the norm, but rare so far - could be a one-off
PlayerCharts.legendPlainNot: You don't play this hand that way
PlayerCharts.sbLimpTitle: How you limp from the SB
PlayerCharts.sbLimpIntro: Hands you complete the blind with a call from the SB when it folds to you. In gray - what you limp, with a counter. Limping weak hands here is normal, not a leak.
PlayerCharts.openIntro: A rough picture across your whole sample - which hands you open first in and from where. It's a mirror, not a template: the hands you open wide light up in lime.
PlayerCharts.legendLimpPlayed: You limp this hand from the SB (with a counter)
PlayerCharts.legendWide: Wide open - worth a closer look
PlayerCharts.legendWideThin: Wide open, but still rare - maybe a misclick
PlayerCharts.reliable: Built from your whole sample (tournaments counted: {count}).
PlayerCharts.preliminary: Tournaments counted so far: {count}. The picture is preliminary - it gets more accurate from about {threshold} tournaments.
